summary: A second version of a proposed mail box protocol, designed as a subset of the File Transfer Protocol. Each site would have a write-only sequential file to which messages and documents sent over the network are appended, to be printed or used later. This was an early step toward network mail. It was replaced by RFC 278.

plainLanguage.summary: Every computer gets a special mailbox file where anyone on the network can drop notes. The owner reads them later. It was an early idea for sending messages between computers.

subtitle: An early proposal for sending messages and documents across the ARPANET

tldr.problem: The Network Information Center needed a way to deliver documents and messages to remote sites without knowing each site's file system conventions, and to receive documents from remote sites for cataloging.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 221 proposes a Mail Box Protocol that lets any site append messages to a standardized, write-only sequential file at another site using a subset of the File Transfer Protocol, with optional control codes for printer formatting.
tldr.outcome: This was an early step toward network email, but it was limited to one-way delivery and did not support the interactive exchange that later became SMTP. It was replaced by RFC 278.

today: RFC 221 is historic and obsoleted by RFC 278. It was an early step toward network email but remained limited to one-way document delivery. This design influenced the development of later mail protocols, though SMTP ultimately took a different approach with interactive two-way communication.

sections.title: Overview
sections.content:
RFC 221 proposes the Mail Box Protocol, version 2, in August 1971. It is a mechanism for delivering messages and documents to remote sites without requiring knowledge of each site's file system conventions. The protocol defines a standardized way to send documents across the ARPANET using a write-only sequential file called a mail box.

The RFC builds on earlier work (RFC 196) but changes the approach to align more closely with the File Transfer Protocol rather than requiring a separate protocol. Multiple mail boxes (numbered 0 to 255) are allowed at each site.
sections.plainLanguage: Someone had an idea for how computers could mail documents to each other. The mail goes into special files that only accept new messages added at the end.

sections.title: Mail Box Design and Format
sections.content:
A mail box is a write-only (from the network) sequential file to which messages and documents are appended. The standard mail box (mail box 0) assumes a line printer 72 characters wide and 66 lines per page. Messages use Network ASCII and the Telnet line ending convention (carriage return plus line feed). Form feed characters move to a new page.

For mail box 0, senders must include an address string at the head of the message with the sender's and receiver's names and addresses in an easy-to-read format for a clerk. The format of information in other mail boxes (1-255) is not defined by the protocol, leaving room for special applications.
sections.plainLanguage: The mail box is designed for a printer: 72 characters wide, 66 lines per page. Messages need the sender and receiver's address at the top so someone can deliver them.

sections.title: Operation and Protocol
sections.content:
The only basic operation required is append: a sender makes an append request, sends the file data (which may span multiple transactions), indicates end of file, and receives an acknowledgment. The data type defaults to Network ASCII and control codes can be used to change printer settings.

The RFC lists control opcodes (change data type, error, acknowledge, append request, printer control settings) and printer control codes (set line width, page size). The protocol uses the Official Initial Connection Protocol and File Transfer Protocol conventions but reserves a specific socket for mail delivery to avoid conflicts with file transfer naming conventions.
sections.plainLanguage: To send mail, you ask for permission to add to the mail box, send your message, and the computer sends back a yes or no. You can also tell the printer how wide to make lines or how big to make pages.
